title: Act IV, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: The Witches brew their potion ('Double, double toil and trouble'). Macbeth demands answers. Three apparitions warn him to beware Macduff (an armed head), tell him none of woman born shall harm him (a bloody child), and that he will never be vanquished until Great Birnam Wood comes to high Dunsinane Hill (a child crowned, with a tree in his hand). He then sees a show of eight kings followed by Banquo's ghost, the last king holding a glass. Learning from Lennox that Macduff has fled to England, Macbeth vows to seize Fife and kill his wife and children.

context.history: The line of eight kings honors the Stuart ancestors of James I; the glass (mirror) may have reflected King James himself if he watched a performance.

significance: Each prophecy is literally true and deeply misleading. Macbeth's decision to kill Macduff's family shows how far he has fallen: 'The very firstlings of my heart shall be the firstlings of my hand.'

satQuestions.passage:
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! beware Macduff;
Beware the thane of Fife. Dismiss me. Enough. Descends.
Whate’er thou art, for thy good caution, thanks;
Thou hast harp’d my fear aright: but one word more—
He will not be commanded: here’s another,
More potent than the first.
Thunder. Second Apparition: A bloody Child.
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth!
Had I three ears, I’ld hear thee.
Be bloody, bold, and resolute; laugh to scorn
The power of man, for none of woman born
Shall harm Macbeth. Descends.
Then live, Macduff: what need I fear of thee?
But yet I’ll make assurance double sure,
And take a bond of fate: thou shalt not live;
That I may tell pale-hearted fear it lies,
And sleep in spite of thunder.
Thunder. Third Apparition: a Child crowned, with a tree in his hand.
What is this
That rises like the issue of a king,
And wears upon his baby-brow the round
And top of sovereignty?
Listen, but speak not to’t.
Be lion-mettled, proud; and take no care
Who chafes, who frets, or where conspirers are:
Macbeth shall never vanquish’d be until
Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill
Shall come against him. Descends.

anchorPassages.note: The hell-broth that will feed Macbeth’s next assurances.
anchorPassages.text:
Round about the cauldron go;
In the poison’d entrails throw.
Toad, that under cold stone
Days and nights has thirty-one
Swelter’d venom sleeping got,
Boil thou first i’ the charmed pot.
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
Fillet of a fenny snake,
In the cauldron boil and bake;
Eye of newt and toe of frog,
Wool of bat and tongue of dog,
Adder’s fork and blind-worm’s sting,
Lizard’s leg and owlet’s wing,
For a charm of powerful trouble,
Like a hell-broth boil and bubble.
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn and cauldron bubble.

anchorPassages.note: He demands knowledge even if nature’s germens tumble.
anchorPassages.text:
By the pricking of my thumbs,
Something wicked this way comes.
Open, locks,
Whoever knocks!
Enter Macbeth.
How now, you secret, black, and midnight hags!
What is’t you do?
A deed without a name.
I conjure you, by that which you profess,
Howe’er you come to know it, answer me:
Though you untie the winds and let them fight
Against the churches; though the yesty waves
Confound and swallow navigation up;
Though bladed corn be lodged and trees blown down;
Though castles topple on their warders’ heads;
Though palaces and pyramids do slope
Their heads to their foundations; though the treasure
Of nature’s germens tumble all together,
Even till destruction sicken; answer me
To what I ask you.

anchorPassages.text:
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! beware Macduff;
Beware the thane of Fife. Dismiss me. Enough. Descends.
Whate’er thou art, for thy good caution, thanks;
Thou hast harp’d my fear aright: but one word more—
He will not be commanded: here’s another,
More potent than the first.
Thunder. Second Apparition: A bloody Child.
Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth!
Had I three ears, I’ld hear thee.
Be bloody, bold, and resolute; laugh to scorn
The power of man, for none of woman born
Shall harm Macbeth. Descends.
Then live, Macduff: what need I fear of thee?
But yet I’ll make assurance double sure,
And take a bond of fate: thou shalt not live;
That I may tell pale-hearted fear it lies,
And sleep in spite of thunder.
Thunder. Third Apparition: a Child crowned, with a tree in his hand.
What is this
That rises like the issue of a king,
And wears upon his baby-brow the round
And top of sovereignty?
Listen, but speak not to’t.
Be lion-mettled, proud; and take no care
Who chafes, who frets, or where conspirers are:
Macbeth shall never vanquish’d be until
Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill
Shall come against him. Descends.

segments.script: Today's words: scepters — rods carried by kings as a sign of power; pricking — a tingling feeling; vanquish — to defeat completely; exploits — bold deeds; boasting — bragging. “vanquish”: Origin: Middle English venquysshen; earlier Old French veincre. “exploits”: Origin of “exploit”: Old French esploit.

words.definition: rods carried by kings as a sign of power
words.sentence:
I’ll see no more:
And yet the eighth appears, who bears a glass
Which shows me many more; and some I see
That two-fold balls and treble scepters carry:
Horrible sight!

By the pricking of my thumbs,
Something wicked this way comes.

Be lion-mettled, proud; and take no care
Who chafes, who frets, or where conspirers are:
Macbeth shall never vanquish’d be until
Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill
Shall come against him.

Time, thou anticipatest my dread exploits:
The flighty purpose never is o’ertook
Unless the deed go with it: from this moment
The very firstlings of my heart shall be
The firstlings of my hand.

No boasting like a fool;
This deed I’ll do before this purpose cool.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Double, double toil and trouble; / Fire burn, and cauldron bubble” slowly and put it in my own words: Around the cauldron, the witches chant "double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble." Next, craft. I notice the strong four-beat rhythm and rhyme, unlike the play's usual blank verse, which marks it as a spell. The strongest word is “cauldron”: it is the pot where their horrible ingredients brew, the source of the visions they will show. Then, effect. What mood does the witches' chant create as Macbeth comes to them? My answer: The chant creates a supernatural, threatening mood; Macbeth now seeks the witches himself, and the prophecies they brew will give him false confidence.

segments.script: Annotate the scene for imagery, structure (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the apparitions and false security? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act IV, Scene I develops the idea of the apparitions and false security. Theme link: the riddles give Macbeth "security," and he resolves to kill Macduff's family immediately. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: Is the foreshadowing in “Act IV, Scene I” effective in presenting the apparitions and false security, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

contentNotes.teacherNote: The witches' recipe includes 'Liver of blaspheming Jew', 'Nose of Turk and Tartar's lips' and 'Finger of birth-strangled babe / Ditch-deliver'd by a drab'. Name the antisemitic and ethnic othering as period prejudice that marks the brew as evil by association; decide in advance that these lines are not performed or read aloud for effect, and discuss why the play links outsiders with evil.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What does the recipe show about who the play treats as 'other'?”
